entities.name: Nalanda University
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
Nalanda University was the world's first residential university and one of the greatest centers of learning in the ancient world, located in Bihar, India. Flourishing from the 5th to 12th centuries CE, it attracted students and scholars from China, Korea, Japan, Tibet, Mongolia, Turkey, and Sri Lanka, teaching subjects including philosophy, logic, mathematics, astronomy, medicine, and Buddhist studies to 10,000 resident students taught by 2,000 teachers.

Founded during the Gupta Empire in the 5th century CE, Nalanda received royal patronage from emperors Kumāragupta and Harsha, who built separate monasteries and libraries. The Chinese pilgrim Xuanzang visited in 637 CE and described the university in detail: eight halls, 300 lecture rooms, observatory, library (called Dharmaganja — 'Treasury of Truth'), and dormitories requiring every applicant to pass entrance exams. His account is the primary historical source for Nalanda's scale and curriculum.

Nalanda was destroyed in 1193 CE by the army of Bakhtiyar Khilji, a commander of the Delhi Sultanate, who burned the libraries — reportedly burning for three months, consuming the greatest collection of Buddhist manuscripts in existence. The destruction of Nalanda effectively ended Buddhism's intellectual dominance in the Indian subcontinent, scattering the monastic scholarly tradition to Tibet and Southeast Asia. A new Nalanda University was established by the Indian government in 2010, reopening in 2014 near the original site.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Nalanda as the world's first residential university created the model for institutional higher education, and its 1193 destruction by fire represents one of history's greatest losses of human knowledge.
